name: Transportation
purpose: Individually authored episode questions and coverage boundaries for Transportation. The subject progression is organized by concrete content rather than a topic-by-angle multiplication.

topics.question: How can a transport system be evaluated by access rather than vehicle movement alone?
topics.coverage: Compare journeys to work, care, education and services using official data and consented accounts; distinguish speed from usable opportunity.

topics.question: What changes between measuring a trip and measuring a whole day's travel needs?
topics.coverage: Map connected activities, transfers, waiting and care responsibilities; avoid treating one commute as every person's mobility pattern.

topics.question: Why can a short trip still be inaccessible?
topics.coverage: Examine crossings, cost, surfaces, assistance, safety and information using user-defined needs; distinguish physical distance from practical access.

topics.question: How does crossing design affect walking time and access?
topics.coverage: Use official design guidance, observed conditions and consented user perspectives; avoid engineering conclusions from photographs alone.

topics.question: What makes a cycling network more than disconnected protected segments?
topics.coverage: Map continuity, junctions, destinations and maintenance through public plans; distinguish installed length from a demonstrated useful network.

topics.question: How can street space be compared across movement, deliveries and public use?
topics.coverage: Use measured dimensions, official policy and varied local accounts; avoid assuming one allocation is best for every place.

topics.question: Why can children and adults experience the same walking route differently?
topics.coverage: Compare sightlines, crossings, time and accompaniment with appropriate consent; do not expose children's routines or treat one family as representative.

topics.question: What does frequent bus service offer that a timetable with a few fast trips cannot?
topics.coverage: Compare waiting, transfers, span and reliability with current official data; distinguish average speed from useful access throughout the day.

topics.question: How can bus priority change passenger journeys without widening a road?
topics.coverage: Inspect signal, lane and stop designs through official evaluations; separate demonstrated corridor outcomes from universal claims.

topics.question: Why can a poorly designed transfer outweigh gains on either side of a journey?
topics.coverage: Trace walking, wait, information, fare and accessibility in a dated example; avoid assuming a mapped connection is feasible for everyone.

topics.question: How can transit routes balance coverage and frequency under a fixed budget?
topics.coverage: Use an explicit illustrative network, demand and access goals; distinguish a planning tradeoff from a personalized service recommendation.

topics.question: What does induced-demand research measure after road capacity changes?
topics.coverage: Inspect original study design, network scope, horizon and alternatives; avoid asserting that every road project has an identical effect.

topics.question: How can congestion be distinguished from unreliability and lack of travel options?
topics.coverage: Compare travel-time distributions, access and mode alternatives using official metrics; avoid treating a single rush-hour image as a complete diagnosis.

topics.question: What changes when a ride service is shared, privately booked or integrated with public transport?
topics.coverage: Compare occupancy, waiting, empty travel, fares and accessibility; verify current terms and avoid universal sustainability rankings.

topics.question: Why can parking policy affect a street beyond the vehicles already parked there?
topics.coverage: Use official data and original studies on circulation, land use, access and revenue; distinguish measured effects from political preference.

topics.question: How do passenger and goods movements compete for the same urban space?
topics.coverage: Map deliveries, stopping, loading windows and user access through official plans; avoid treating all freight as a removable inconvenience.

topics.question: What determines whether cargo can shift between road, rail and water?
topics.coverage: Compare terminals, load form, schedule, handling and infrastructure with documented cases; distinguish theoretical connectivity from an available service.

topics.question: How can last-mile delivery be evaluated beyond the speed of the final courier?
topics.coverage: Trace sorting, failed delivery, access, labor and return trips; use primary data where available and do not invent efficiency rates.

topics.question: What does transport affordability mean when household time and income differ?
topics.coverage: Compare fares, mandatory transfers, total trips and time costs with official methods; avoid one fixed threshold being presented as universally sufficient.

topics.question: How can a mobility study include people who stay home because travel is difficult?
topics.coverage: Use ethical surveys, access needs and missing-trip questions; distinguish observed ridership from all potential demand.

topics.question: Why can gendered travel-pattern research require care about household roles and context?
topics.coverage: Inspect sampling, trip chains, safety perceptions and within-group variation; avoid predicting an individual's needs from gender.

topics.question: How can rural transport be studied without using urban frequency as the only benchmark?
topics.coverage: Compare dispersed destinations, service days, assistance and local accounts; distinguish low density from absence of public responsibility.

topics.question: What must be defined before comparing the emissions of two transport modes?
topics.coverage: Specify occupancy, energy source, route, infrastructure and lifecycle boundary; distinguish global averages from local operating conditions.

topics.question: Why can electric vehicles change tailpipe emissions without resolving every transport impact?
topics.coverage: Compare energy, materials, tires, land use and access using primary evidence; avoid either zero-impact marketing or dismissing documented benefits.

topics.question: How can road-safety performance be compared without confusing exposure with raw crash counts?
topics.coverage: Use official definitions, travel measures, severity and reporting completeness; avoid declaring a road safe from a low count alone.

topics.question: What does a safe-system approach change about assigning responsibility after a crash?
topics.coverage: Read official framework documents and evaluated interventions; distinguish systemic prevention from removing individual legal accountability.

topics.question: How can a transport appraisal include benefits and costs borne by different groups?
topics.coverage: Use official methods, explicit distribution and uncertainty; avoid presenting one monetary total as the complete public decision.

topics.question: What should be checked before accepting an autonomous-mobility demonstration as evidence of broad capability?
topics.coverage: Inspect operating domain, intervention, authorization and actual trial data; distinguish a staged route from general operation.

topics.question: How can a city compare a pilot mobility service with a long-term commitment?
topics.coverage: Track subsidy, access, reliability, data rights and evaluation design; distinguish uptake during free trials from durable demand.

topics.question: How should a transport explainer report a project that exists only as an announcement?
topics.coverage: Separate proposal, approval, funding, construction and operation with dated official records; avoid drawing a proposed line as an available route.

science.requirements: Use original observations or experiments, an appropriate scientific reference and the actual measurement method. Distinguish mechanisms, correlations, model assumptions, uncertainty and limits of generalization.
source_leads: original research reports and data
research-institution observation records
methods papers and current scientific reference works

community.requirements: Use consented participant accounts, local records and the community's own descriptions. Include differences of position, access and power; testimony is not a representative survey or clinical proof.
source_leads: consented interviews and oral histories
community publications and local records
field notes with method and consent documented

civic.requirements: Use the current official legal text, policy, procedure or public dataset for a specific jurisdiction and date. Distinguish written rules, implementation and lived access; give no personal legal or financial conclusion.
source_leads: official laws, rules and administrative guidance
audits, judgments and public service records
consented accounts from affected people and qualified specialists

technical.requirements: Use the actual system documentation, a worked implementation and measurements. Identify inputs, outputs, constraints, tolerances, failure conditions and the limits of the example. Do not provide hazardous construction or unauthorized access procedures.
source_leads: original engineering papers
official versioned product or standards documentation
test reports and drawings with clear provenance
